■ INTRODUCTION
Alcohols are ubiquitous in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, fra‐
grances, and flavorings and also serve as indispensable syn‐
thetic intermediates in both laboratory and industrial setings.<sup>1,2</sup>
Accordingly, the development of eficient and selective synthetic
strategies for functionalized alcohols remains a subject of endur‐
ing interest and practical importance.<sup>3</sup> In organic chemistry,
epoxides occupy a privileged position owing to their easy prep‐
aration and intrinsic ring strain, which renders them suscepti‐
ble to reductive or nucleophilic ring-opening reactions.<sup>4</sup> On
the other hand, organic electrosynthesis has re-emerged as a
powerful and sustainable platform for redox transformations,
leveraging electrons as traceless reagents to generate reactive
intermediates under mild and environmentally benign condi‐
tions.<sup>5</sup> Electrochemical transformations of epoxides have also
started to atract atention: Lu and co-workers disclosed the
electroreduction of epoxides with carefully tuned proton sources
suppressing hydrogen evolution to enable regioselective access
to Markovnikov alcohols from alkyl epoxides (Scheme 1A-i)
and anti-Markovnikov alcohols from aryl or benzyl epoxides
(Scheme 1A-ii).<sup>6</sup> Qiu et al. and Zhang et al. independently ach‐
ieved electrocarboxylation of aryl epoxide with carbon dioxide,
afording β-hydroxy carboxylic acids with a very high selectivity
(Scheme 1A-iii).<sup>7</sup> These studies collectively underscore the deci
sive influence of the substitution on the reactivity and selectivity
of epoxides.<sup>8</sup>
We envisioned that the incorporation of an alkynyl moiety
could unlock new reactivity paterns of epoxides. The first
thing that came to our mind is their two-component coupling
reactions with organic halides, which may potentially furnish a
new methodology for the syntheses of diferent functionalized
two-component alcohols, i.e., allenols P1, homopropargylic alco‐
hols P2, or propargylic alcohols P3 (Scheme 1B, top). This
design is accompanied by formidable challenges (Scheme 1B,
botom): (i) the simultaneous presence of two strained C−O
bonds raises the challenge of competing cleavage of two distinct
C−O bonds; (ii) the incorporation of an alkyne substituent
complicates the regioselectivity, owing to the presence of multiple
reactive sites that can engage in coupling with aryl halides;<sup>9</sup> (iii)
direct electroreduction of the alkynyl epoxide represents a facile
but undesired pathway forming mono-component allenols BP1,
homopropargylic alcohols BP2, and propargylic alcohols BP3 as
reported in the literature;<sup>6</sup> (iv) possible allenols P1 or propargyl
alcohols P3 are susceptible to over-reduction<sup>10</sup> or cyclization<sup>11</sup>
under electrochemical conditions.

We reasoned that merging transition metal catalysis with
electrochemistry could overcome these obstacles by afording
greater control over bond activation, regioselectivity, and product
distribution.<sup>12,13</sup> Such a merger ofers complementary advantages:
electrochemistry provides a tunable and sustainable means to
generate reactive intermediates, while transition metal catalysis
governs their selective capture and subsequent transformation.
The synergy between these two activation modes can orchestrate
complex redox sequences that are dificult to achieve by either
approach alone. In this context, Shi et al. demonstrated an elegant
nickel-catalyzed electroreductive coupling of alkyl epoxides with
aryl halides in the presence of isopropyl chloroformate as a CO
surrogate (Scheme 1A-iv).<sup>14</sup> Herein, we report the first example
of nickel-catalyzed electrochemical two-component coupling of
alkynyl epoxides with organic halides (Scheme 1C). The current
protocol enables eficient and exclusive synthesis of structurally
diverse allenols,<sup>15</sup> a very important class of compounds accommo‐
dating an array of synthetically reactive groups without protection
and deprotection.

With the optimized conditions in hand, we first evaluated
the substrate scope of aryl halides, and the structures of the
resulting allenol products were unambiguously confirmed through
the X-ray single-crystal analysis of allenol 3ka (Scheme 2). Both
electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups at the ortho-
(3ac and 3af), meta- (3ab, 3ae, 3bg, and 3ah), and para-positions
(3aa, 3ad, 3aj, 3ak, 3cl, 3cm, 3an, 3ao, 3bp, 3bq, 3ar, 3as, and
3bt) of iodobenzenes are compatible, yielding the corresponding
α-allenols in moderate to good yields exclusively. Steric efects
play a role since the ortho-substituted aryl iodides provided lower
yields (3ac vs 3aa, 3ab; 3af vs 3ad, 3ae). A wide array of functional
groups, such as alkoxyl (3ac and 3ca), phenyl (3ak), chloride
(3ar), trifluoromethyl (3as), nitrile (3bt), naphthyl (3bu), and
pendant benzoheterocycles (3av and 3aw), were well-tolerated
under the current conditions. Notably, substrates with reactive
functional groups such as hydroxyl (3an), Boc-protected amine
(3ao), carboxylate (3bp), and bromide (3ad) all delivered the
α-allenols in 59−67% yields, underscoring the excellent scope of
this strategy.
To further probe chemoselectivity, bifunctional substrate 2q
bearing both an electrophilic C−I bond and a nucleophilic
C−B bond was evaluated, afording allenol 3bq in 50% yield.
This outcome highlights the strong preference of those electro‐
chemical conditions for cross-electrophile coupling over electro‐
phile−nucleophile pathways. Gratifyingly, the substrate scope
was further extended to heteroaryl halides. 7-Iodoquinoline (2x)
as well as 3-iodopyridines (2y and 2z) participated smoothly,
delivering allenols 3ax−3az in good yields. In addition to aryl
iodides, aryl bromides also performed well, afording α-allenols
3aA−3aD smoothly when the electrolyte was switched from NaBr
to NaI. To facilitate product purification, the reactions of 2A and
2B were carried out on a 0.2 mmol scale under a constant current of
2 mA. Notably, 3-bromoquinoline was also successfully engaged to
furnish product 3aD. Atempts to further extend the scope of aryl
halide substrates to aryl chlorides proved unsuccessful, as neither
p-methoxy nor p-methoxycarbonyl-substituted phenyl chloride
aforded the allenol product (Table S5). However, particularly
noteworthy is the selective reactivity observed with bromophenyl
iodides, where the transformation occurred exclusively at the C−I
bond to furnish the corresponding allenols (3ad−3af) while leav‐
ing the C−Br bond untouched. Such chemoselective activation of
aryl iodides over the C−Br bond in the same molecule represents
a valuable feature for further stepwise elaboration, enabling the
streamlined synthesis of aryl bromide-flanked allenol scafolds that
can serve as versatile intermediates for further cross-coupling or
functionalization transformations.
The generality of the reaction was further extended to vinyl
bromides, enabling the synthesis of alkenyl allenes: Cyclic
vinyl bromides, including cyclopentenyl (3aE) and cyclohex‐
enyl derivatives (3aF), as well as benzene-fused analogues
(3aG and 3aH), underwent smooth conversion under the stand‐
ard conditions.

■ CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, we have developed an electro-driven
nickel-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling reaction of alkynyl
epoxides with aryl/alkenyl halides, which allows for the efficient
construction of diverse α-allenols while tolerating a wide range
of synthetically useful functional groups. This method represents
a compelling alternative to conventional approaches that rely
on preformed nucleophiles such as Grignard reagents,<sup>24−26</sup> orga‐
nozinc species,<sup>27,28</sup> organoboron reagents,<sup>29−32</sup>
and terminal
alkynes.<sup>33,34</sup> These traditional allenol synthesis sufers from limi‐
ted functional group tolerance due to the high reactive nature
of the organometallic reagents. Although organoboron reagents
are relatively stable and less reactive, their tedious preparation
using highly reactive reagents further restricts functional group
compatibility. This protocol exhibits high regioselectivity and a
distinctive selectivity profile, featuring preferential C−O bond
activation over C−X bonds as well as pronounced chemoselectiv
ity for C−I activation. Notably, this strategy can be applied to the
synthesis of allenols incorporating biologically relevant motifs
under mild conditions and demonstrated that allenols can serve
as valuable intermediates for further synthetic transformations.

\dot { \bf N } { \bf a } _ { 2 } S { \bf O } _ { 4 } ,
